blocks.text: 1. Multi-Agent RAG System
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448213544-728713811.png

Real-Time News Assistant closed by pointing toward a stable, slowly changing knowledge base as a better fit for a simpler design. Multi-Agent RAG System, a design where several coordinated agents each handle a distinct part of a complex task, assembles the specialist agent techniques covered earlier in this course into one complete, working system.
It assembles specialist agents into one working system rather than a single monolithic pipeline.
2. The Design Problem's Scope
Unlike every earlier design in this module, one single retrieve-then-generate pipeline cannot handle this task's full complexity.
The task naturally splits into distinct roles, each better handled by its own specialist.

blocks.text: 3. A Coordinator Agent Routes Work To Specialists

blocks.alt: A Coordinator Agent Routes Work To Specialists
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448213544-101447857.png
As with a coordinator assigns work to specialists in Multi-Agent Systems, one coordinator agent decides which specialist agent handles which piece of an incoming request.
A research specialist, a retrieval specialist, and a writing specialist each focus on just their own role.
4. Each Specialist Agent Has Its Own Tools And Retrieval Scope

blocks.alt: Each Specialist Agent Has Its Own Tools And Retrieval Scope
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448213545-291589727.png
As with each agent can have its own tools and memory in Multi-Agent Systems, a retrieval specialist needs search tools the writing specialist never touches.
Scoping tools and retrieval access per agent keeps each one focused and simpler to reason about.
5. Agents Pass Results Along The Pipeline

blocks.alt: Agents Pass Results Along The Pipeline
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448213546-88554057.png
As with agents pass results to one another in Multi-Agent Systems, the retrieval specialist's gathered evidence becomes the writing specialist's actual input.
The same dependency chain, now assembled into one working end-to-end system.

blocks.text: 6. A Review Agent Checks Output Before It Reaches The User

blocks.alt: A Review Agent Checks Output Before It Reaches The User
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448213546-799038716.png
As with reflection across agents, not just within one, in Multi-Agent Systems, a dedicated reviewer agent can catch a poorly grounded draft before the user ever sees it.
That same reflection technique becomes this system's actual final quality gate.

7. Coordination Overhead Grows With Each Added Agent

blocks.alt: Coordination Overhead Grows With Each Added Agent
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448213547-95546217.png
As with coordination overhead grows with agent count in Multi-Agent Systems, every additional specialist adds real coordination and latency cost to the whole pipeline.
The number of agents should match the actual complexity of the task, not be added for its own sake.
8. Tracing Requests Across Multiple Agents For Visibility
A single request now touches several agents, each its own logical stage.
The same distributed tracing lets a developer see the whole multi-agent flow end to end.
9. Recognizing When This Specific Multi-Agent RAG Design Fits The Actual Need

blocks.alt: Recognizing When This Specific Multi-Agent RAG Design Fits The Actual Need
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448213547-558849020.png
A task naturally splitting into distinct specialist roles fits this design.
A simple, single-purpose retrieval task fits a naive or single-agent pipeline better instead.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates a coordinator routing to retrieval and writing specialists with a review agent as the final gate.

code.content:
def retrieval_specialist(query):
    # each specialist agent has its own tools and retrieval scope
    return "Falcon plan costs twenty dollars per month, includes ten projects."

def writing_specialist(evidence, query):
    # agents pass results along the pipeline
    return f"Based on the available information: {evidence}"

def review_agent(draft):
    # a review agent checks output before it reaches the user
    if "based on" not in draft.lower():
        return False, "Draft lacks a clear grounding reference."
    return True, "Approved"

def coordinator(query):
    # a coordinator agent routes work to specialists
    evidence = retrieval_specialist(query)
    draft = writing_specialist(evidence, query)
    approved, reason = review_agent(draft)
    if not approved:
        return f"Rejected by reviewer: {reason}"
    return draft

print("Multi-agent RAG system example:")
print(coordinator("What does the Falcon plan cost?"))

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the request flowing from retrieval to writing to review before reaching the final output, exactly the coordinated, multi-stage pipeline as a multi-agent RAG system.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Forcing a simple, single-purpose task through an unnecessary multi-agent pipeline.
Giving every agent the same broad tool access instead of scoping tools per specialist role.
Skipping a review agent, letting a poorly grounded draft reach the user unchecked.
Adding agents without tracing, losing visibility into which stage a request is actually in.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: A multi-agent RAG system splits a complex task across several coordinated specialist agents.
A single retrieve-then-generate pipeline cannot handle a task that naturally splits into distinct roles.
A coordinator agent decides which specialist handles which piece of an incoming request.
Each specialist agent is scoped to its own tools and retrieval access, keeping it focused.
One agent's output becomes the next agent's input, forming a real dependency chain.
A dedicated review agent catches a poorly grounded draft before it reaches the user.
Every additional agent adds real coordination and latency cost, so agent count should match complexity.
Distributed tracing across agents gives visibility into the whole multi-agent request flow.
